A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and retain corresponding algorithms, theoretical results, and proofs. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 3.1 and Figure 1 report original runtime experiments comparing bisection, Newton, and MOSEK under two regularizers.

after.justification: Section 3.1 reports runtime experiments, and Appendix B adds original cumulative-regret simulations in stochastic and adversarial settings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects its stated FTRL update to use the current context Xt instead of historical Xs and the actual optimization variable. Section 3 adds a partition-matroid adaptation using a separate scalar solve per partition. The central entropy-FTRL, matrix-resampling, and bisection procedures remain intact.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic projection-runtime tests, Appendix B evaluates sequential, context-free m-set bandit learning in stochastic and adversarial environments. This substantially expands the evaluated task requirements, although it does not add empirical evaluation of the contextual or corrupted-stochastic setting.

E2.justification: Newton and MOSEK remain the evaluated comparison methods. Appendix B uses the same comparator set in Tables 2–3, although its trajectory plots show only bisection and MOSEK. Table 1 compares published theoretical bounds and introduces no experimentally evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The retained runtime experiment changes its stated loss range from [-1,1] to [0,1] and tolerance from 10^-9 to 10^-7. Appendix B introduces cumulative-regret evaluation over 10,000 rounds, with m in {3,5}, K in {20,40}, and gap 0.0625. These are substantial additions to the evaluation design; the PDFs do not establish how the new environments generate losses.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a substantive implementation-validation analysis: it tests whether replacing direct MOSEK projection with bisection preserves OSMD's regret trajectories across regularizers, environments, and configurations. Tables 2–3 also include Newton. V1 assessed computational speed without this corresponding learning-behavior check.

E5.justification: The runtime experiment retains its 25-iteration description and 95% confidence-interval reporting. New Tables 2–3 add mean-plus/minus-sigma regret summaries. The regret experiments do not disclose repetition counts or seeds, so no increase in repeated runs can be established.

E6.justification: Appendix B adds regret trajectories and final outcomes; for example, Table 2 reports stochastic regret of 711.3 ± 146.3 for bisection versus 734.5 ± 143.0 for MOSEK at K=20, m=3 under Tsallis regularization. Figure 1's runtime curves also change, and the stated speed-up over MOSEK falls from approximately 20-fold to five-fold. Because the runtime settings change, this is not a same-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: The main regret rates and convergence theorems are retained, but several definitions and proofs change. V2 broadens the formal action-set definition, defines gaps using expected linear losses, corrects the Appendix A.1 Bregman gradient and Lemma 2.4's equality to an upper bound, revises Lemma 2.5's cardinality reasoning, and corrects the projection proof's root condition from zero to m. It also adds a brief partition-matroid complexity argument.

C1.justification: The first-BOBW-algorithm claim and principal regret orders remain unchanged. The contribution statement now explicitly distinguishes general combinatorial regret guarantees from projection acceleration for m-sets, while identifying separable action sets as extensions. This refines the stated scope of the computational contribution.

C2.justification: Section 3 newly explains why partition separability preserves computational efficiency. Appendix B interprets regret similarity as implementation validation and asserts agreement up to numerical tolerance, although the tabulated means differ. The two principal limitations concerning logarithmic overhead and dependence on m remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds a project repository link advertised as providing code to reproduce all figures; v1 only links the Newton baseline's repository. V2 removes the detailed CVXPY implementation and runtime-fairness footnote while retaining the Python, processor, and MOSEK Fusion API disclosures.

R1.justification: V2 adds a cross-setting theoretical comparison in Table 1 and citations to Ito et al. (2022) on feedback graphs and Oxley (2011) on matroids. It removes the Diamond and Boyd (2016) CVXPY reference. The three-part related-work narrative and central novelty positioning otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The section sequence and Appendix A proof organization are preserved. Changes consist mainly of local wording and terminology corrections, author/header edits, author-year citations, and short explanatory additions, including the new Appendix B.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with a theoretical comparison table, four paired regret-trajectory figures, and two final-regret tables. It also reformats the document into the ICLR conference template and resizes the retained runtime figure. These changes extend well beyond pagination or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: The added regret checks and reproduction-code link improve validation and reproducibility beyond v1's timing-only evidence, while corrections to the contextual update and several mathematical formulas remove explicit errors. The gains are limited: Appendix B evaluates context-free OSMD, leaves loss generation and repetition counts unspecified, and overstates numerical agreement despite differing tabulated means. It strengthens the computational contribution without comprehensively validating the contextual BOBW algorithm.
